routes.label: Find the digit before the final zero

question: In a certain card game, a player is dealt a hand of \(10\) cards from a deck of \(52\) distinct cards. The number of distinct (unordered) hands that can be dealt to the player can be written as \(158A00A4AA0.\) What is the digit \(A?\)
solution:
The digit immediately before the final zero is \(A\), so dividing the hand count by \(10\) lets us find \(A\) using only a units-digit calculation.

Let \(N\) be the number of hands. A hand is an unordered selection of ten distinct cards, so
\[
N=\binom{52}{10}
=\frac{52\cdot51\cdot50\cdot49\cdot48\cdot47\cdot46\cdot45\cdot44\cdot43}
{10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7\cdot6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1}.
\]
The division by \(10!\) removes the different orderings of the same ten cards.

Cancel \(48\) with \(8\cdot6\) and \(45\) with \(9\cdot5\). The remaining denominator factors \(4,3,10,7,2\) divide \(52,51,50,49,44\), respectively. This gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
N&=13\cdot17\cdot5\cdot7\cdot47\cdot46\cdot22\cdot43\\
&=10\cdot17\cdot13\cdot7\cdot47\cdot46\cdot11\cdot43.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(N\) has decimal form \(158A00A4AA0\), the units digit of \(N/10\) is \(A\).

A product's units digit depends only on the units digits of its factors. Writing \(\equiv\pmod{10}\) to mean equal remainders upon division by \(10\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac N{10}
&\equiv7\cdot3\cdot7\cdot7\cdot6\cdot1\cdot3\\
&=(7\cdot3)(7\cdot3)(7\cdot6)\cdot1\\
&\equiv1\cdot1\cdot2\cdot1=2\pmod{10}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore \(\boxed{A=2}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
The repeated digit \(A\) controls both the final digits and the digit sum, so divisibility tests can determine it without evaluating the entire hand count.

Let \(N\) be the number of unordered ten-card hands. Then
\[
N=\binom{52}{10}
=\frac{52\cdot51\cdot50\cdot49\cdot48\cdot47\cdot46\cdot45\cdot44\cdot43}
{10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7\cdot6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1}.
\]
Cancel \(48\) with \(8\cdot6\), and \(45\) with \(9\cdot5\). The other denominator factors \(2,3,10,7,4\) divide \(52,51,50,49,44\), respectively, leaving
\[
N=26\cdot17\cdot5\cdot7\cdot47\cdot46\cdot11\cdot43.
\]
Only \(26\) and \(46\) are even, and each contains exactly one factor of \(2\). Thus \(N\) is divisible by \(4\), but not by \(8\). None of the displayed factors is divisible by \(3\), so neither is \(N\).

Because \(100\) is divisible by \(4\), divisibility by \(4\) depends only on the last two digits. Those digits are \(A0\), representing \(10A\). Therefore \(A\) must be even. Among the listed choices, this leaves \(2,4,6\).

If \(A=4\), the last three digits are \(440\), which is divisible by \(8\). Since \(1000\) is also divisible by \(8\), this would make \(N\) divisible by \(8\), a contradiction.

If \(A=6\), the digit sum of \(158A00A4AA0\) is
\[
1+5+8+4+4A=18+24=42.
\]
A number is divisible by \(3\) exactly when its digit sum is divisible by \(3\). This would make \(N\) divisible by \(3\), another contradiction.

The only remaining choice is \(\boxed{A=2}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
